citeAs: Clark, P., Cowhey, I., Etzioni, O., Khot, T., Sabharwal, A., Schoenick, C., and Tafjord, O. (2018). Think you have Solved Question Answering? Try ARC, the AI2 Reasoning Challenge. arXiv:1803.05457.
creator: Peter Clark, Isaac Cowhey, Oren Etzioni, Tushar Khot, Ashish Sabharwal, Carissa Schoenick, Oyvind Tafjord (Allen Institute for Artificial Intelligence)
description: The AI2 Reasoning Challenge (ARC) is a question set of 7,787 natural, grade-school science questions (multiple choice, authored for human standardized tests) partitioned into a Challenge Set (2,590 questions answered incorrectly by both a retrieval-based and a word co-occurrence algorithm) and an Easy Set (5,197 questions). It is designed to require far more powerful knowledge and reasoning than previous QA challenges, and is accompanied by the ARC Corpus of 14M science-related sentences.
name: ARC (AI2 Reasoning Challenge)
rai:dataBiases: The Challenge Set is defined operationally by two specific baseline solvers (IR and PMI), which only approximates the informal goal of "hard" questions. Questions are drawn from US elementary and middle school science curricula, limiting the subject domain. A large portion of questions (about 43% of ARC) come from a single anonymous content partner (Mercury). The dataset includes the publicly releasable subset (~60%) of the Kaggle 2016 Allen AI Science Challenge questions, which may introduce selection bias. Grade-level difficulty labels overlap substantially, as each grade contains a mixture of easy and difficult questions.
rai:dataCollection: Questions were drawn from a variety of standardized test sources (grade-school science exams authored for human tests), including state assessments (e.g., ACTAAP, AIMS, MCAS, NY Regents, TIMSS) and an anonymous content partner (Mercury). The collection involved several months of extensive search and investigation to obtain publicly releasable questions. The dataset includes the publicly releasable subset (~60%) of the 2016 Allen AI Science Challenge (Kaggle) questions, making up 43% of the ARC set.
rai:dataCollectionRawData: Natural science questions authored for standardized tests, drawn from a variety of sources including state and national assessments (ACTAAP, AIMS, Alaska Dept Ed, AMP, CA Standards Test, FCAT, LA Ed Assessment Program, MD School Assessment, MCAS, MEA, MEAP, Mercury, MSA, NAEP, NC READY, NY Regents, Ohio Achievement Tests, TAKS, TIMSS, VA Standards of Learning, WASL). All questions are non-diagram, multiple-choice (typically 4-way), targeting grades 3–9.
rai:dataLimitations: The Challenge Set definition (questions answered incorrectly by both IR and PMI solvers) only approximates the informal goal of "hard" questions. Questions are restricted to non-diagram, multiple-choice science questions for grades 3–9, limiting generalizability. The dataset does not cover diagram-based questions. Most questions come from US standardized tests, limiting geographic and cultural diversity. The ARC Corpus, while covering ~95% of Challenge question knowledge, may not provide sufficient signal for simple retrieval methods to answer the questions correctly.
rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: Questions were partitioned into a Challenge Set and an Easy Set using two baseline solvers: (1) an Information Retrieval (IR) solver using the Waterloo corpus and Elasticsearch, and (2) a Pointwise Mutual Information (PMI) solver. Questions answered incorrectly by both solvers were placed in the Challenge Set (2,590 questions); the remainder formed the Easy Set (5,197 questions). The dataset was further split into train/dev/test partitions.
rai:dataSocialImpact: ARC is intended to drive progress in AI research toward more advanced question answering requiring reasoning and knowledge, moving beyond factoid retrieval tasks. The authors pose it as a community challenge with a public leaderboard to encourage broad participation. Progress on ARC would represent a significant step forward for the AI community in developing systems capable of deeper language understanding and reasoning.
rai:dataUseCases: Benchmarking advanced question answering systems that require knowledge and reasoning beyond simple retrieval or word co-occurrence methods. Intended to encourage AI research in advanced question answering, particularly for questions requiring multi-hop reasoning, commonsense knowledge, and deeper text comprehension. Includes a leaderboard for community participation.
rai:machineAnnotationTools: IR solver (Elasticsearch-based retrieval using the Waterloo corpus) and PMI (Pointwise Mutual Information) solver were used to partition questions into Challenge and Easy sets. These automated algorithms determined which questions were "hard" (Challenge Set) vs. "easy" (Easy Set).
